findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema is built from invalid computed keys and strips all fields except access_token
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the same literal string (`"[object Object]"` – ZodString has no toString override), so the resulting schema is effectively `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown }`. It does not validate the expiry at all, and because `z.object` strips unknown keys, parsing a real token response in credential-sharing mode returns only `{ access_token }` – `expires_in`/`expiry_date`/`refresh_token` are discarded. Every caller that writes `tokenResponse.data` into the credential key will therefore persist a credential with no expiry and no refresh token, breaking subsequent refreshes.

findings.title: Fake refresh_token placeholder overwrites valid stored refresh tokens
findings.body: When the parsed response has no `refresh_token` (common: Microsoft/Office365 and others only return one sometimes, and the schema marks it optional), the code assigns the literal string `"refresh_token"`. Callers spread `tokenResponse.data` over the stored credential key (e.g. office365calendar CalendarService), so the previously valid refresh token is replaced by the dummy string and all future token refreshes for that user fail permanently, requiring re-installation of the app.

findings.title: Credential key is written as a SafeParseReturnType object instead of the parsed key
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the zod `safeParse` result (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed value, yet the result is stored directly: `data: { key }`. Previously `googleCredentialSchema.parse()` returned the key object. This persists `{"success":true,"data":{...}}` into `credential.key`, which no longer matches `googleCredentialSchema`, so Google Calendar breaks for the user after the first token refresh.

findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in salesforce CalendarService
findings.body: `prisma.credential.update(...)` is called in `getClient`, but the file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a ReferenceError (or a TS compile error) hit on every Salesforce calendar operation, making the integration completely non-functional.

findings.title: Salesforce token is refreshed unconditionally on every client creation and the new token is not used
findings.body: `getClient` now performs a refresh_token request on every instantiation regardless of expiry (extra latency and Salesforce rate-limit pressure), and then builds the jsforce Connection with the *old* `credentialKey.access_token`/`instance_url` instead of the freshly obtained `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`. So the refresh is wasted work and an already expired access token is still used.

findings.title: Response success checked via `statusText !== "OK"`
findings.body: `response.statusText` is empty for HTTP/2 responses and is not guaranteed to be "OK" otherwise. Using it as the success check can throw an HttpError with an empty message on perfectly successful refreshes. Use `response.ok`/`response.status` instead.

findings.title: refreshOAuthTokens returns heterogeneous types; callers expecting axios/googleapis shapes break when sync is enabled
findings.body: In the sync branch the function returns a raw `fetch` Response, while in the fallback branch it returns whatever the provider SDK returns (an axios response with `.data` for hubspot/zohocrm/zoho-bigin, `fetchTokens.res` for googleapis, a Response for fetch-based apps). With credential sharing enabled, hubspot does `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` on a Response (NaN expiry), zoho reads `tokenInfo.data.error` (undefined) and persists a Response-shaped object as the credential key, and googlecalendar reads `res.data` (undefined). Each affected app needs to parse the sync endpoint response consistently.

findings.title: Request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is unauthenticated and the response status is never checked
findings.body: The POST to the self-hoster's sync endpoint carries no shared secret/authorization header, so any party able to reach that endpoint can request tokens for an arbitrary `calcomUserId`; symmetrically Cal.com has no way to verify it is talking to the right endpoint. The returned Response is also forwarded without checking `response.ok`, so a 4xx/5xx body is passed to parsing/persistence paths.

findings.title: credentialId passed where userId is expected in refreshOAuthTokens
findings.body: `refreshAccessToken(credentialId, credentialKey)` passes `credentialId` as the third argument of `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, appSlug, userId)`. With credential sharing enabled the sync endpoint will be called with `calcomUserId = <credential id>`, returning tokens for the wrong user (or failing). The credential's `userId` must be plumbed through instead.

findings.title: appSlug "zoomvideo" does not match the Zoom app slug used elsewhere
findings.body: The credential/app slug for Zoom is `zoom` (see `createOAuthAppCredential({ appId: "zoom", ... })` in zoomvideo/api/callback.ts and the webhook handler which looks up `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug } })`). Passing `"zoomvideo"` to `refreshOAuthTokens` means the self-hosted endpoint receives a slug that does not exist in the app store, so self-hosters can't correlate it with the slug they must send back to `/api/webhook/app-credential`.

findings.title: Unvalidated zod parse and missing HTTP method check cause 500s instead of 400s
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError for malformed payloads, which surfaces as an unhandled 500 rather than a 400 with a useful message. Likewise `symmetricDecrypt`/`JSON.parse` on line 57-59 will throw on a bad ciphertext or wrong key. There is also no method restriction, so a GET with the right secret reaches the body parse. Wrap in try/catch and use `safeParse` plus a `req.method !== "POST"` guard.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time equality and no length guard
findings.body: The shared secret is compared with `!==`, which short-circuits and leaks timing information; for a long-lived static secret this is a realistic oracle for an attacker who can send many requests. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on buffers of equal length. Additionally, `req.headers[...]` may be a string array when the header is sent twice; that case silently fails rather than being rejected explicitly.

findings.title: Existing invalid credentials are not revalidated and multiple credentials are ignored
findings.body: When updating an existing credential only `key` is set; if the credential had previously been flagged `invalid: true` (e.g. by the zoom/webex invalidateCredential paths), it stays invalid and the freshly synced keys will never be used. Set `invalid: false` on update. The `findFirst` also silently ignores additional credentials for the same user/app, leaving stale duplicates that other code paths may pick up.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean
findings.body: `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` evaluates to `string | undefined`, so the exported constant has a misleading name and type for a flag that is consumed in boolean contexts and could be serialized/compared elsewhere. Wrap in `!!(...)`.

findings.title: Diagnostic logging for failed Outlook token refresh removed
findings.body: The previous code logged the zod error and the raw Microsoft response when the refresh token response failed validation. Now `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws a generic `new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` with no provider detail, making Outlook refresh failures much harder to diagnose in production.
